page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Integrate using the linear substitution rule
steps.margin_note: First mark. Because the coefficient of x inside the root is negative (−2), the antiderivative carries a negative sign.
steps.memory_tip: ∫dx/√(a−bx) = −(2/b)√(a−bx) + c — the minus sign always shows up when x has a negative coefficient.
steps.why: The linear expression inside the root has derivative −2, so the antiderivative picks up a factor of −1/2 in front of the usual 2√(...) form, giving −√(3−2x).
common_mistakes: Using a positive sign instead of the negative sign that comes from differentiating 3−2x.
Forgetting the factor −1/2 altogether and writing √(3−2x) directly.

steps.label: Apply the limits
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Subtracting a negative lower-limit value effectively adds √3.
steps.memory_tip: √3 ≈ 1.73, so √3−1 is a small positive number — a useful check on the sign.
steps.why: Substituting the upper limit x=1 gives −√1=−1, and subtracting the lower-limit value −√3 (i.e. adding √3) gives the final result √3−1.
common_mistakes: Losing track of the double negative when subtracting the lower-limit value.
Computing √(3−2) as √1=1 but forgetting the leading minus sign in front.
